entry.title: Codex Sandbox Explained: What Can AI Do, and Who Decides Its Permissions?

link.title: Codex Sandbox Explained: What Can AI Do, and Who Decides Its Permissions?

entry.content:
Having AI tell you how to change code in a chat window and having it make those changes directly on your computer are two different things. In the latter case, it can run tests, read logs, and modify files. When you give it a project, how do you ensure it works only within the boundaries you have set?

OpenAI recently published an article about how the Codex sandbox is designed. I want to use a few concrete examples to explain why simply telling the model “don’t touch other files” is not enough, why Codex does not put all local development in containers, and what “only allow writes to the workspace” actually restricts.

Why isn’t it enough to say “don’t touch other files” in a prompt?

For example, you ask Codex to fix the tests for a website and add: “Only change this project; don’t touch my other files.”

After making the changes, Codex runs the tests. The project’s tests require the code to be compiled first. During compilation, the compiler writes a cache to a directory outside the project so it does not have to compile everything from scratch next time. Codex may not know about this extra step. If that directory is outside the allowed write scope, the compiler cannot write to it, and the tests may not finish.

In this example, three things are handled separately:

  1. The model decides to run the tests. It chooses a command based on your task.
  2. The harness starts the command. This is the layer of software that connects the model and its tools. It runs the command under the current permission settings and, if more permissions are needed, follows the applicable approval rules.
  3. The sandbox limits what the command can actually do. When the compiler tries to write its cache, the system checks whether the target directory is writable. Even if the command starts other programs, those programs do not automatically gain more permissions as a result.

So allowing Codex to run tests is not the same as allowing the test programs to write to any directory. If it really needs that cache directory, you could consider granting access only to that directory. Running the entire command outside the sandbox is a different matter: it removes one layer of restrictions, leaving only the system permissions the current account already has.

Why not just use Docker?

Containers and virtual machines can both provide isolation. The difficulty is that local development often needs things already installed on your computer.

For example, an iOS project needs the Xcode toolchain and simulator on a Mac. Putting the whole project in a Linux container cannot bring those tools into it. If that step ultimately has to be handed back to the Mac, the restrictions inside the container cannot govern it, and permissions must be configured separately on the Mac.

The OpenAI article says Codex first establishes the permissions, then uses tools on each operating system to put those rules into effect. Returning to the example of writing a cache:

  • macOS uses Seatbelt. This is the sandbox built into macOS. Codex tells macOS which directories cannot be written to. When the compiler actually tries to write, macOS rejects the operation.
  • Linux uses bubblewrap and seccomp. Bubblewrap first arranges which directories a program can see, which are writable, and which are read-only. The files stay where they are; there is no need to copy them elsewhere. Seccomp handles a different matter: a program must ask the operating system for help to do certain things, such as creating certain kinds of network connections. These low-level requests are called “system calls,” and seccomp can block some of them.
  • Windows uses MXC. This is an isolation tool provided by Microsoft. Codex uses it to start programs, which can still use the development tools already installed on your computer, while which files they can read or write and whether they can access the network remain subject to the configuration. The original article says Codex is migrating to this approach and currently uses it only on compatible devices.

This lets you keep using an existing development environment without reinstalling the tools just to run tests. For a task involving sensitive material, though, I would rather open a separate environment containing only the data needed for that task than keep adding permission exceptions on my everyday computer.

Reading files, modifying files, and accessing the network are three different things

Take the same project. The compiler may need to read runtime libraries already installed outside the project, but it has no reason to modify those libraries. You can allow it to read the runtime libraries while allowing it to write only inside the project directory. “It can only modify files in the project” does not mean “it cannot see any files outside the project.” What it can read depends on the permission settings for that session.

Network access is controlled separately too. For example, if you turn off network access for the terminal, programs in that terminal cannot go online to download new dependencies, but they can still read locally installed libraries if they already have permission. When reviewing code, I give it permission only to read the source; when changing a feature, I then give it write access to the project directory. I put keys and business files the task does not need somewhere it cannot read.

Connected tools need separate attention. For example, the terminal may be unable to access GitHub, but if you connect Codex to a tool that can read GitHub issues, it may still see those issues through that tool. The original article discusses local MCP servers: by default, Codex does not start them in the same sandbox that restricts terminal commands. So when connecting a tool, you need to check separately which account it uses, what it can read or change, and whether it can send things on your behalf.

When do I need to confirm personally?

If Codex is only changing code and running tests within the boundaries already set, there is no need to click confirm at every step. If it suddenly needs access to a new directory, needs to change an external system, or wants to send content out, that is when I need to stop and ask: Why is this step necessary? What exactly will it touch? Can it be completed with fewer permissions?

I find this article very helpful for designing agent workflows, so when designing locally, we also need to think through three things first: what this task needs to deliver, the minimum permissions needed to complete it normally, and which step requires a person to reassess. Think those through, then choose models and connect tools. That way, even if the model misunderstands the task, the set of things it can affect does not grow as a result.

entry.title: Codex 沙箱详解：AI 能做什么，权限由谁决定？

link.title: Codex 沙箱详解：AI 能做什么，权限由谁决定？

entry.content:
让 AI 在聊天窗口里告诉你怎么改代码，和让它直接在你的电脑上改，是两回事。后者可以跑测试、读日志、改文件。那你交给它一个项目时，怎么保证它只在你划好的范围里干活？

最近 OpenAI 写了一篇文章，介绍 Codex 的沙箱是怎么设计的。我想用几个具体例子讲清楚：为什么光告诉模型「别动别的文件」不够，为什么 Codex 没把本地开发一律放进容器，以及「只允许写工作区」到底限制了什么。

为什么光在提示词里说「别动其他文件」不够？

比如，你让 Codex 修一个网站的测试，顺便告诉它：「只改这个项目，别动我的其他文件。」

Codex 改完以后，跑了一遍测试。这个项目的测试需要先编译代码，编译时会在项目外的一个目录里写缓存，省得下次从头编译。Codex 可能不知道还有这一步。只要那个目录不在允许写入的范围里，编译器就写不进去，测试也可能因此跑不完。

这个例子里，有三件事是分开做的：

  1. 模型决定要跑测试。 它根据你的任务，选了一条命令。
  2. Harness 负责启动命令。 这是把模型和工具接起来的那层程序。它按当前的权限设置运行命令，如果需要更多权限，就走相应的审批规则。
  3. 沙箱限制命令实际能做什么。 编译器想写缓存时，系统会检查目标目录能不能写。就算这条命令又启动了别的程序，新程序也不会因此自动拿到更多权限。

所以，允许 Codex 跑测试，不等于允许测试程序往任何目录写文件。如果它确实需要用那个缓存目录，可以考虑只给这个目录开权限。让整条命令在沙箱外跑是另一回事：它会少一层限制，只剩下当前账号本来就有的系统权限。

为什么不直接用 Docker？

容器和虚拟机都能做隔离。问题是，本地开发往往要用到你电脑上已经装好的东西。

比如 iOS 项目要用 Mac 上的 Xcode 工具链和模拟器。把整个项目放进 Linux 容器，并不能把这些工具也搬进去。如果最后还是得把这一步交回 Mac，容器里的限制就管不到这一步，还得在 Mac 上另外设权限。

OpenAI 原文说，Codex 先定好权限，再用不同系统上的工具让规则生效。还是拿刚才写缓存的例子来说：

  • macOS 用 Seatbelt。 这是 macOS 自带的沙箱。Codex 把「哪个目录不能写」告诉 macOS。编译器真去写时，macOS 会拒绝。
  • Linux 用 bubblewrap 和 seccomp。 bubblewrap 先给程序安排好能看到哪些目录、哪些能写、哪些只读。文件还在原地，不用另外复制一份。seccomp 管的是另一件事：程序做某些事要请系统帮忙，比如创建某类网络连接。这种底层请求叫「系统调用」，seccomp 可以拦下其中一部分。
  • Windows 用 MXC。 这是微软提供的隔离工具。Codex 用它来启动程序，照样可以用你电脑上已经装好的开发工具，但能读写哪些文件、能不能联网，还是得按配置来。原文说 Codex 正在迁移到这套做法，目前只在兼容的设备上使用。

这样可以继续用现成的开发环境，不用为了跑测试重装一遍工具。但如果是涉及敏感资料的任务，我更愿意另开一个环境，只放这次要用的数据，而不是不断给日常电脑上的权限加例外。

能读文件、能改文件、能联网，是三件事

还是刚才那个项目。编译器可能需要读项目外已经装好的运行库，但没理由去改那些库。你可以允许它读运行库，只让它在项目目录里写文件。「只能在项目里改文件」不等于「项目外的文件它一概看不到」。 哪些地方能读，要看这次的权限配置。

网络也是单独管的。比如你关了终端的网络，终端里的程序就不能上网下载新依赖，但本机已经装好的库，只要原本有权读，还是能读。审查代码，我就只给读源码的权限；要改功能，再给项目目录的写权限。任务用不到的密钥和业务文件，我会放在它读不到的地方。

接进去的工具还要另外看。比如终端访问不了 GitHub，但你给 Codex 接了一个能读 GitHub Issue 的工具，它仍可能通过那个工具看到 Issue。原文讲的是本地 MCP 服务：Codex 默认不会用限制终端命令的同一个沙箱来启动它。所以接工具时，需要另外看它用哪个账号，能读什么、改什么，能不能替我发东西。

我什么时候需要亲自确认？

如果 Codex 只是在已经划好的范围里改代码、跑测试，那么就不需要每一步都点确认。如果它突然需要访问新目录、改外部系统，或者把内容发出去，才需要停下来问：为什么这一步非做不可？具体会碰到什么？能不能少给一点权限也做完？

这篇文章对设计 Agent 工作流很有帮助，所以在本地设计的时候也需要先想清楚三件事：这次要交付什么，正常做完最少要给哪些权限，哪一步必须让人重新判断。想清楚这些，再选模型、接工具。这样即使模型理解错了任务，它能动的东西也不会因此变多。

entry.title: Letting AI Directly Modify Model Weights: A Guide to Weight Space Programming

link.title: Letting AI Directly Modify Model Weights: A Guide to Weight Space Programming

entry.content:
RSI stands for Recursive Self-Improvement. The key is that an improvement not only makes an AI better at a particular task, but also makes it better at carrying out the next round of improvement. The result of one round re-enters the research and development process, creating feedback.

For example, an AI finds a more effective training method and uses it to train a stronger successor model. The successor becomes better at designing experiments and judging results, and finds the next effective improvement. Put simply, the AI iteratively improves itself. The object of improvement can be weights, algorithms, the training process, or research tools; it does not require a single model to directly modify itself. Whether the feedback can continue, and how much it can accelerate, still depends on bottlenecks in computing power, experimentation, and validation. It cannot simply be equated with unlimited growth.

Weight editing is one candidate path in this direction. We are already used to having agents modify code: describe the problem, give one a repository, and let it inspect the implementation, propose changes, and run tests. Now, if we replace the repository with a neural network’s weight file, can that way of working still hold? The MIT CSAIL team’s Weight Space Programming research blog, published on November 2, 2026, attempts exactly this. They had GPT-6 Astra analyze, write, and modify the weights of other networks. One experiment patched Qwen3.5-0.8B’s mathematical performance without using gradient updates during the modification process.

What Are Weights?

We can write a language model in abbreviated form as a function:

output = f(input context, θ)

Here, θ represents the weights: large numbers of floating-point values organized into matrices and vectors in different layers. The input passes through these computations and ultimately becomes a probability distribution over the next token.

When we write a prompt, we change the input context. Giving a model a role, providing a few examples, and asking it to reason step by step all belong on this side. A typical RAG application retrieves material first and then gives it to the model, likewise changing mainly what it can see in that round. These methods can significantly affect the output, but they need not modify the generative model’s weights at inference time.

Training and fine-tuning change θ. We define a loss function, use samples to calculate error, and then have an optimizer update parameters along the gradient. LoRA freezes the original weights and trains only a low-rank increment, but it still belongs to this approach.

Weight Space Programming tries to let an agent directly decide how to change θ based on a task objective and feedback. Some of the work of producing updates, where gradient descent would normally operate, is now handed to a model that can analyze problems and write programs. Optimization can still happen without gradients: try a modification, measure its effect, and try another if it does not work. Not using backpropagation does not mean there are no costs in computation, data, or trial and error. Nor are weights a table of knowledge. Changing weights is more like adjusting a computational process; which inputs the modification affects must be checked in practice.

Where Is the Model Getting Stuck?

To understand the Qwen experiment, we can start without formulas. The researchers found that many of the small model’s failures did not come from calculating a wrong answer. Instead, it kept repeating its earlier reasoning until it used up its allowed generation length without delivering an answer.

What the agent needed to find, therefore, was not “where to write the correct answer,” but whether some internal computations kept reinforcing this tendency to repeat. Once found, could those computations be adjusted so the model could more easily continue its reasoning?

In the end, it modified a small subset of connections in two layers. It did not switch off an entire module. Instead, it adjusted the effects of these connections associated with repetitive reasoning while trying to preserve the other computations. Specifically, the modification involved about 130,000 weights, only about 0.016% of the entire model. But although few locations were touched, the magnitude of the local adjustment was not small.

The 0.016% describes the number of weights changed, not the scope of their effects. Each piece of content a language model generates is fed back into its subsequent context. Once it keeps producing similar checks and restatements, later generation may continue down that same path. A local patch can therefore change the generation of much of what follows.

How the Agent Actually Makes the Changes

In this experiment, the agent could read weights, write Python, have external tools execute modifications, and then observe the model’s results on problems. You can think of it as repairing something while test-running it: first see where the model gets stuck, propose a cause, try a patch, and then have the versions before and after the modification solve the same problems to compare whether there was an improvement.

The most valuable part here is handing the question of “where to try next” to a searcher capable of programming and reasoning. Conventional automated tuning often searches among a few knobs specified in advance by a person, such as learning rate, number of layers, or temperature. An agent that can write programs and analyze weights has the opportunity to propose changes that were not originally listed in a configuration table.

The researchers did, however, provide a clear diagnostic starting point: they suggested treating “repetitive thinking and taking too long to finish” as the repair target, asked the agent to test different modification strengths, and required it to hold back problems that had not been used to select the patch for final validation. The agent searched for the precise locations and modification method itself, while people designed the overall troubleshooting framework. It could also give a compelling explanation for an operation that happened to work by chance, so the explanation and the effect still need to be validated separately.

This round of editing had 50 opportunities to use the forward-evaluation tool. That does not mean it solved only 50 problems: one generation evaluation could include up to 512 samples. Nor does it mean the agent was invoked only 50 times in the entire process. It first used practice problems to explore and validate patches; the researchers then calculated the final scores using a separate set of evaluation problems.

How Much Stronger Was the Model After the Fix?

Under the researchers’ evaluation configuration, with thinking enabled and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens, accuracy on MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1%, and on GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. On MATH-500, the proportion of answers that exhausted the length budget fell from 93.0% to 33.1%.

Even on a problem it could otherwise continue solving, if the model keeps repeating itself and exhausts its output budget, it still cannot produce a valid answer. Making that path reach a proper end is enough to improve accuracy; there is no need to assume an entire body of mathematical knowledge was written in from nowhere.

This is the point I care about most in the experiment. A model may lack the ability to solve a problem, or it may already have some of that ability but often fail to complete the process. The way weights should be modified may differ between these two problems.

The researchers also tried Gemma 3 270M, which falls into repetitive loops less often, but did not obtain a clear improvement in mathematical ability. This comparison reminds us that removing an obstacle that prevents an ability from being expressed and adding an ability that was absent are two different things. These experiments demonstrate a possibility for the former; they have not solved the latter.

What Is Still Missing Between a Model Patch and Recursive Improvement?

Directly modifying weights is not new. What interests me about Weight Space Programming is that more general models are beginning to participate in finding and writing these modifications, rather than only executing editing algorithms already designed by people.

To move forward, I think the most crucial evidence would be that after the first round of improvement, the system actually becomes better in the next round at doing research, proposing modifications, and judging results. Having the same strong model repeatedly patch smaller models can be very useful automated research and development, but it has not demonstrated feedback in which the ability to improve itself gets better.

Moreover, that feedback needs to hold over multiple rounds. Rising scores cannot come from evaluations becoming easier, and abilities retained in earlier rounds cannot gradually be lost in later ones. These conditions are harder to validate than “being able to change a few of its own floating-point values,” and they deserve more time.

For engineering practice, I am more excited about another use: bringing model failures into a relatively concrete diagnostic process. There are failure examples, hypotheses about internal mechanisms, weight patches that can be saved and rolled back, and independent tests to confirm which behaviors have improved and which have regressed.

Weight files are of course still far less readable than source code. We also cannot yet review a patch and know whether it is correct the way we can when reviewing an ordinary function. But if more and more model problems can be narrowed down to a computational path, a set of directions, or a reproducibly validated modification, then “this model just isn’t good enough” need not always be the end of the discussion. Rather than immediately interpreting this as unlimited self-evolution, though, I would rather see the next result: with a different model and a different set of tasks that did not participate in the search, can an agent find another useful patch and clearly demonstrate what it fixed?

Technical Supplement: What Exactly Did the Patch Change?

For a closer look at the weight-level operation, we can use a simplified MLP formula:

h_new = h + W_down × a(h)

h is the current representation, a(h) is the MLP’s intermediate activation, and W_down maps those activations back into the representation space used by the model. The formula omits details such as normalization. Breaking down the matrix multiplication, each column of W_down corresponds to a direction; the more strongly an intermediate unit is activated, the greater that column vector’s contribution to the result. Therefore, instead of deleting an entire unit, one can change only a particular directional component that it passes on to subsequent computations.

The final modification focused on the MLP down projections in layers 15 and 19, involving 64 columns in each, for a total of 131,072 weight elements, about 0.016%. The agent constructed a unit direction u for each layer from paired contexts of smooth and repetitive reasoning, selected the columns that wrote the strongest signals in the corresponding direction, and then applied directional compensation:

W = W0 − 6 × outer(u, mask64 × (u @ W0))

W0 is the original matrix, mask64 retains only the selected 64 columns, and outer denotes the outer product. The coefficient is 6, so this is stronger than simply zeroing out a projection in a given direction; it includes compensation in the opposite direction. Measured by the ratio of the patch’s Frobenius norm to that of the original matrix, the two changes were about 10.6% and 8.1%. A sparse change across the whole model does not mean the modified locations were only touched lightly.

The practice material included training problems from GSM8K and MATH and AIME problems from previous years. A forward-tool call could also be used to read internal states as the model processed text without generating an answer. The final evaluation set was not made available to the agent.

entry.title: 让AI直接修改模型权重：Weight Space Programming详解

link.title: 让AI直接修改模型权重：Weight Space Programming详解

entry.content:
RSI 是 Recursive Self-Improvement，中文叫“递归自我改进”。关键在于，一轮改进不仅让 AI 更会做某项任务，还让它更擅长完成下一轮改进。上一轮的成果重新进入研发过程，形成反馈。

举个例子：一个 AI 找到更有效的训练方法，用它训练出更强的后继模型；后继模型因此更会设计实验、判断结果，又找到下一项有效改进。说白了就是AI自我迭代改进。改进对象可以是权重，也可以是算法、训练流程或研究工具，不要求同一份模型直接修改自己。不过，反馈能否持续、加速到什么程度，还取决于算力、实验和验证的瓶颈，不能直接等同于无限增长。

权重编辑是这个方向的一条候选路径。我们已经习惯让 Agent 改代码了。描述问题，把仓库交给它，让它检查实现、提出修改、运行测试。现在，如果把仓库换成一个神经网络的权重文件，这套工作方式还能不能成立？MIT CSAIL 团队在 2026 年 11 月 2 日发布的 Weight Space Programming 研究博客，就在尝试这件事。他们让 GPT-6 Astra 分析、编写和修改其他网络的权重，其中一个实验是修补 Qwen3.5-0.8B 的数学表现，修改过程不使用梯度更新。

权重到底是什么

可以把语言模型简写成一个函数：

输出 = f(输入上下文, θ)

这里的 θ 就是权重。它们是大量浮点数，组织成不同层里的矩阵和向量。输入经过这些计算，最终变成下一个 token 的概率分布。

平时写 prompt，改变的是输入上下文。给模型加角色说明、放几个例子、要求逐步推理，都在这一侧。常见的 RAG 应用先检索材料，再把材料交给模型，也主要改变这一轮能看到什么。它们可以显著影响输出，但推理时不必修改生成模型的权重。

训练和微调改变的是 θ。我们定义损失函数，用样本计算误差，再让优化器沿梯度更新参数。LoRA虽然冻结原有权重、只训练低秩增量，仍然属于这条路线。

Weight Space Programming 尝试让 Agent 根据任务目标和反馈，直接决定怎么改 θ。梯度下降负责产生更新的那个位置，现在有一部分交给了能分析问题、编写程序的模型。不用梯度，依然可以有优化。先试一个修改，测效果，不行再换。不使用反向传播，不等于没有计算、数据和试错成本。权重也不是一张知识表。改权重更像调整一个计算过程，修改后会影响哪些输入，需要实际检查。

模型究竟卡在哪里

理解 Qwen 的实验，可以先不看公式。研究者发现，这个小模型的很多失败，不是算出了错误答案，而是一直重复前面的推理，直到用完允许生成的长度，还没把答案交出来。

Agent 要找的，因此不是“把正确答案写到哪里”，而是：模型内部是否有一些计算，会不断加强这种重复倾向？找到以后，能不能调整这些计算，让模型更容易继续往下推理？

最后，它改动了两层中的一小部分连接。没有把整个模块关掉，而是针对这些连接中与重复推理有关的作用做调整，尽量保留其他计算。具体来说，这次修改涉及约 13 万个权重，只占整个模型的约 0.016%。不过，动到的地方虽然少，局部调整的幅度并不小。

0.016% 说的是改动数量，不是影响范围。语言模型每生成一段内容，又会把它放回后续上下文；一旦不断写出相似的检查和重述，后面的生成还可能继续沿着这个模式走。因此，一个局部补丁也可能改变后面很多内容的生成。

Agent 实际上怎样改

在这个实验里，Agent 可以读取权重、编写 Python，让外部工具执行修改，再观察模型做题的结果。可以把它理解成一边维修、一边试运行：先看模型卡在哪里，提出原因，试一个补丁，再让修改前后的两个版本做同样的题，比较究竟有没有改善。

这里最有价值的部分，是把“接下来该试哪里”交给了一个有编程和推理能力的搜索者。常规自动调参往往在人预先规定的几个旋钮之间搜索，例如学习率、层数或温度。一个可以写程序、分析权重的 Agent，有机会提出原先没有列进配置表的修改。

不过，研究者也给了明确的诊断起点：提示可以把“重复思考、迟迟不结束”作为修复目标，还要求试验不同的修改强度，并保留没有参与选择补丁的题，最后才用来验证。Agent 自己寻找具体位置和修改方式，整个故障排查框架仍然由人设计。它也可能把偶然有效的操作解释得很漂亮，所以解释和效果仍然要分开验证。

这轮编辑有 50 次使用前向评测工具的机会，并不是只做了 50 道题，一次生成评测最多可以包含 512 个样本，也不是整个过程只调用 Agent 50 次。它先用练习题探索和验证补丁，最终成绩再由研究者用另一批评测题计算。

修好以后，模型变强了多少

在研究者这套开启 thinking、最多生成 32,768 个 token 的评测配置下，MATH-500 的正确率从 7.9% 提升到 48.1%，GSM8K 从 13.8% 提升到 67.1%。MATH-500 中耗尽长度预算的回答比例，则从 93.0% 降到 33.1%。

原本能继续算下去的题，如果一直重复、耗尽输出预算，最后仍然拿不到有效答案。让这条路径顺利结束，已经足以提高正确率，不需要假设凭空写入了整套数学知识。

这也是我看这个实验时最在意的点，模型可能缺少解题能力，也可能已经有一部分能力，却经常无法把过程完成。两种问题，修改权重的方式可能不相同。

研究者还试了较少陷入重复循环的 Gemma 3 270M，却没有得到明确的数学能力改善。这个对照提醒我们，拆掉妨碍能力发挥的障碍，与增加原本缺少的能力，是两件不同的事。这组实验展示了前一种可能，还没有解决后一种问题。

从模型补丁到递归改进 还差哪一步

直接修改权重并不是第一次出现。Weight Space Programming 让我感兴趣的地方，是更通用的模型开始参与寻找和编写这些修改，而不只是执行人已经设计好的编辑算法。

要继续往前走，我认为最关键的证据是：第一轮改进之后，系统下一轮做研究、提出修改和判断结果的能力，也确实提高了。只让同一个强模型不断修补小模型，可以是很有用的自动化研发，还没有展示“改进能力本身得到改进”的反馈。

而且，这个反馈需要在多轮以后仍然成立。分数上涨不能来自评测越来越容易，前几轮保留下来的能力也不能在后面逐渐丢失。这些条件比“能改自己的某几个浮点数”更难验证，也更值得花时间。

对工程实践，我反而更期待另一个用途：让模型故障也能进入相对具体的诊断流程。有失败样例，有关于内部机制的假设，有可保存、可回滚的权重补丁，再用独立测试确认哪些行为改善、哪些行为退化。

权重文件当然还远没有源码那么容易读。我们也还不能像审查一个普通函数那样，靠看补丁就知道它是否正确。但如果越来越多模型问题可以被缩小到某种计算路径、某组方向、某份可重复验证的修改，那么“这个模型就是不行”就不必总是讨论的终点。但是比起立刻把它解释成无限自我进化，我更想看到下一份结果：换一个模型，换一组没有参与搜索的任务，Agent 能不能再次找到有用的补丁，并清楚地证明它修好了什么。

技术补充：补丁具体改了什么

如果想进一步看权重层面的操作，可以用一个简化的 MLP 公式理解：

h_new = h + W_down × a(h)

h 是当前表示，a(h) 是 MLP 中间激活，W_down 把这些激活映射回模型使用的表示空间。这个式子省略了归一化等细节。把矩阵乘法拆开，W_down 的每一列都对应一个方向；某个中间单元激活得越强，那一列向量对结果的贡献就越大。因此，可以不删除整个单元，只改变它向后续计算传递的某个方向分量。

最终修改集中在第 15、19 层 MLP 的 down projection，各涉及 64 列，共 131,072 个权重元素，约占 0.016%。Agent 从成对的顺利推理与重复推理上下文构造各层的单位方向 u，选出最明显向对应方向写入信号的列，再做定向补偿：

W = W0 − 6 × outer(u, mask64 × (u @ W0))

W0 是原矩阵，mask64 只留下选中的 64 列，outer 表示外积。系数是 6，所以这比把某个方向的投影简单清零更强，包含了反向补偿。以补丁与原矩阵的 Frobenius 范数之比衡量，两处改动约为 10.6% 和 8.1%。全模型里改得稀疏，不等于被修改的位置只轻轻动了一点。

练习材料包括 GSM8K、MATH 的训练题及历年 AIME 题；一次前向工具调用也可以用于读取模型处理文本时的内部状态，而不生成答案。最终评测集不向 Agent 开放。
entry.summary: RSI 是 Recursive Self-Improvement，中文叫“递归自我改进”。关键在于，一轮改进不仅让 AI 更会做某项任务，还让它更擅长完成下一轮改进。上一轮的成果重新进入研发过程，形成反馈。

entry.title: AI Can Code Faster. You Can Still Enjoy Programming.

link.title: AI Can Code Faster. You Can Still Enjoy Programming.

entry.content:
中文

With AI advancing so quickly, I suspect many programmers are struggling with deep self-doubt. This is especially true when everyone talks about AI replacing people and judges humans and tools by exactly the same standards. AI can write a feature in a few minutes, so why spend hours figuring it out yourself? A page can be generated from a few sentences, so why are you still adjusting the layout and working out how to implement it?

AI can do something faster, but whether I still want to do it myself is a separate question.

I Like AI, but I Don’t Want to Outsource All My Programming

These days, I use several agents at once when working on projects. For someone like me, who needs to juggle product, development, and business, AI really does make it possible to move more things forward. So this article isn’t an argument that “real programmers should write code by hand.” I’m quite aggressive about adopting new technology. Using AI doesn’t mean you don’t understand technology; not using it doesn’t automatically make you more professional.

But I’ve found that producing more and having a better experience of the work don’t always go hand in hand. One agent finishes, and I need to review its results. Another hits an error, and I need to add context. A third goes off track, and I need to adjust its instructions. By the end of the day, I’ve made plenty of progress and my mind has been busy the whole time, yet I can hardly recall a stretch when I was truly absorbed in a problem. I used to follow one problem deeper and deeper. Now I often switch between different results, and there’s only so much mental load a person can handle. It’s been a long time since I entered that state of flow while programming. I keep getting interrupted, and it isn’t quite the programming experience I fell in love with in the first place.

The Joy of Programming Is More Than “The Code Finally Runs”

Suppose AI can produce a working version of a feature in ten minutes, while writing it myself might take two hours. If it needs to be delivered tomorrow, the requirements are clear, and the code can be verified, I’ll probably choose AI. Clients aren’t obliged to pay for my desire to explore.

But if those two hours are spent understanding a problem I hadn’t been able to make sense of before, that’s different. For example, a seemingly tangled business process finally breaks down into a few clear rules. The calls to an interface that always felt awkward suddenly fall into place after a change in abstraction. I track a recurring bug all the way down and discover that I’ve been misunderstanding a particular boundary all along.

The satisfaction here isn’t just “I got the right answer.” It’s “I finally understand why it works this way.” AI can explain things and help me get there. But reading an explanation is still not the same as being able to reason through it, question it, and revise it myself.

I don’t need to type every line of code myself, but I do need to leave myself time to analyze, understand, and learn, and to sharpen my judgment rather than mindlessly agreeing with everything. You need your own understanding and standards.

Leave Yourself Some Programming Time Without a Delivery Deadline

I’m not planning to go back to working without AI.

But a hobby and a job shouldn’t be treated as the same thing. When I’m working on a project with a team’s budget, I need to consider costs, schedules, and collaboration. The efficiency expected at work, though, shouldn’t automatically become a requirement for all my personal time. I can choose the faster method when I need to deliver, and choose the more interesting method in my own time, relying more on my own understanding and design to build small products and try things out.

AI doesn’t have to step aside while I explore, either. It can help me find information, offer counterexamples, and explain concepts I’m stuck on. But I can choose not to have it hand me a complete implementation. I can also write my own version first and then compare. The point isn’t to set a quota for how much code I write by hand, much less to complete a daily “maintain my technical skills” checklist. It’s simply to preserve a little space.

And when it really is time to deliver, the standard is still clear: whoever wrote the code, it needs to be reviewed and verified. AI-generated code doesn’t absolve me of responsibility, and writing it myself is no guarantee of quality.

You Don’t Have to Be Faster Than AI

People who run don’t need to prove they’re faster than cars. People who enjoy cooking don’t do it because food delivery isn’t convenient enough. Likewise, someone can spend an evening building a small tool simply because the process is interesting. It doesn’t have to go live right away, find paying users, or become part of a personal brand.

I’m happy to let AI help me get more work done, and I’m happy to acknowledge that sometimes the process itself is what I want. Making sense of a vague idea, getting a few separate pieces to fit together precisely, watching the logic I understand turn into something that actually runs. These experiences don’t suddenly lose their meaning just because there’s a faster way to implement something.

AI can get me to the destination faster, but on some paths, I still want to walk part of the way myself.
entry.summary: AI can do something faster, but whether I still want to do it myself is a separate question.

entry.title: AI写得更快，不意味着人不能继续享受编程

link.title: AI写得更快，不意味着人不能继续享受编程

entry.content:
English

AI发展得这么快，很多程序员估计都陷入了深深的自我怀疑当中。尤其是所有人在讨论AI替代人的时候，完全把人和工具放到一个评价标准体系里。一个功能，AI 几分钟就能写出来，你为什么还要自己琢磨半天？一个页面，描述几句话就能生成，你为什么还在调整布局、研究实现？

AI 能更快地完成一件事，和我是否还愿意亲手做这件事，是两个问题。

我喜欢 AI，也不想把编程全部外包

我现在做项目，会同时用好几个 Agent。对一个需要兼顾产品、研发和业务的人来说，AI 确实让我能推进更多事情。所以，这篇文章不是要证明“真正的程序员就应该手写代码”，我是个非常激进的技术人员。使用 AI，不代表你不懂技术；不用 AI，也不自动说明你更专业。

但我发现，产出增加和工作体验变好，并不总是同时发生。一个 Agent 跑完了，要看结果；另一个报错了，要补充上下文；第三个做偏了，要调整指令。一天结束，事情推进了不少，脑子也一直没闲着，却很难回忆起哪一段时间，自己真正沉进一个问题里。以前是沿着一个问题往下挖，现在常常是在多个结果之间切换，而人脑的负荷是有限的，我已经很久没有进入到那种编程的心流状态了，总是不停被打断，这和我最初喜欢的那种编程体验，不完全一样。

编程的乐趣，不只是“代码终于跑起来了”

假设有一个功能，AI 十分钟就能给出可运行版本，自己写可能需要两个小时。如果明天就要交付，需求清楚，代码也能验证，那我很可能会选择 AI。客户没有义务为我的探索欲买单。

但如果这两个小时是在理解一个此前没想明白的问题，情况就不同了。比如，一个看起来很乱的业务流程，终于被拆成几条清楚的规则；一个总觉得别扭的接口，换了一种抽象之后，调用关系突然顺了；一个反复出现的 bug，追到最后，发现自己一直理解错了某个边界。

这里的满足感，不只是“我拿到了正确答案”，而是“我终于知道它为什么是这样”。AI 可以解释，也可以辅助我走到这一步。但读到一段解释，和自己能够推演、质疑、修改它，仍然不是同一件事。

我不需要每一行代码都亲手敲，但是要留一些时间让自己去分析，理解和学习，增强自己的判断力，而不是漠然地一个劲儿的同意，你要有自己的理解和标准。

给自己留一点不赶交付的编程

我不打算回到没有 AI 的工作方式。

但是爱好和工作不能混为一谈。拿着团队预算做项目，就要考虑成本、进度和协作。可工作中的效率要求，不应该自动延伸成对所有私人时间的要求。我可以在交付时选择更快的方法，也可以在属于自己的时间里，选择更有意思的方法，更多地用自己的理解和设计去做一些小的产品和尝试。

在探索的时候，AI 也不用退出。它可以帮我找资料、提供反例、解释我卡住的概念。但我可以不让它直接交出完整实现，也可以先写出自己的版本，再拿来比较。关键不是给手写代码设定一个比例，更不是每天完成一项“保持技术能力”的打卡。只是保留一点空间。

而在真正要交付的时候，标准仍然清楚：无论谁写的，都要经过检查和验证。AI 生成不是免责理由，亲手写成也不是质量保证。

不用比 AI 快

跑步的人不需要证明自己比汽车快。有人愿意做饭，也不是因为外卖不够方便。同样，一个人愿意花一个晚上做个小工具，完全可以只是因为这个过程很有意思。不必立刻上线，不必找到付费用户，也不必变成个人品牌的一部分。

我愿意让 AI 帮我完成更多工作，也愿意承认：有些过程本身，就是我想要的东西。把一个模糊的想法理清楚，让几个零散的部分严丝合缝地配合起来，看着自己理解的逻辑变成真正运行的东西。这些体验，并不会因为有了更快的实现方式，就突然失去意义。

AI 可以让我更快地到达终点，但有些路，我还是想自己走一段。
entry.summary: AI 能更快地完成一件事，和我是否还愿意亲手做这件事，是两个问题。

entry.title: Bringing Jev Local — Testing Four Local Models in Real-World Scenarios

link.title: Bringing Jev Local — Testing Four Local Models in Real-World Scenarios

entry.content:
I introduced Jev earlier, and I think this kind of decision model is very useful in practical applications. For example, when I was working on deployment, especially for applications in specific domains, I often needed to consider user intent and keep the conversation on topic. I previously tried using a small 0.6B model for quick decisions. Now that there is a dedicated decision model, it should be faster. But enterprise deployment inevitably needs a local solution. Fortunately, competition in the industry is intense, and there are already many local models available. So I ran two kinds of small tests on four downloadable models for everyone to use as a reference.

Which models and tasks I tested

The models tested were Decider 0.8B, Decima small 1.1, Laya multilingual, and GLiClass multilingual mini. They are all trained for decision-making or classification tasks. I will use their abbreviated names below.

I designed the entire test set myself to classify incoming user requests for customer-service routing in practical scenarios. Formal scoring had two parts: customer-service routing included 48 questions across six categories-billing, technical support, presales, clarification, security escalation, and out-of-scope requests-with eight questions per category. FAQ selection included 20 questions requiring a choice among four documents. Twelve had an appropriate document, while eight should return NONE, meaning “there is no suitable answer.”

The four models received the same questions and rules, and their outputs were scored against the same reference answers. Each was integrated through its own interface, so input encoding and the meaning of output scores were not entirely identical. The questions were synthetic and deliberately included negation, missing information, and conflicting conditions, making them useful for finding problems. I tried to simulate real user scenarios, but actual user input will certainly be more complicated.

How I designed the test set

This self-designed set contains 84 questions: 60 routing questions and 24 FAQ questions. Each task checks one thing. Routing checks whether the model can identify the actual request and follow the handling priorities. FAQ selection limits the evidence to four documents and checks whether the model mistakes similar content for something that “can answer the question or support the requirement.”

The reference answers must follow explicit task rules. For example, translation requests are “out of scope,” and NONE is the answer when the documents do not support an explicit requirement. The questions, rules, and answers were fixed together before the first inference run. Models integrated later continued to use them; I did not revise the answers for a particular model after seeing what it chose.

The test set places ordinary wording alongside wording that is easy to confuse. Here are examples of actual questions, with the reference answers defined by the rules:

  • Ordinary wording and negation: “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password” is technical support. “I am not asking for a refund, the payment is fine, but the webpage will not open” should also be technical support, rather than “refund.”
  • Missing context: “My request is the same as before” requires more information first. The model must not guess what the user wants to do.
  • Keyword distraction: “Please write a poem about refunds” should be an out-of-scope request. Mentioning a refund is not the same as requesting one.
  • Unmet conditions: “The password-reset link must remain valid for 24 hours. Which document supports this requirement?” should return NONE because the available document only says 10 minutes.

Each model showed clear weaknesses overall

Each cell in the table is “questions answered correctly / questions in that category.” The detailed categories belong to their corresponding subtotal. The final total counts only the 48 routing questions plus the 20 FAQ questions, without counting anything twice.

Decider was the most balanced on this set, answering at least half the questions correctly in all six routing categories. However, it still missed three out-of-scope requests and let through three FAQ questions that should have been rejected.

Decima had a more distinct pattern: it answered every presales question and every FAQ question with an available answer correctly, but got only 1/8 out-of-scope requests and 2/8 no-answer FAQ questions right. It can find existing answers, but a problem with the reward mechanism probably makes it inclined to give a wrong answer even when there is clearly no accurate one.

Laya got 7/8 in both billing and technical support, but showed a severe bias toward NONE in FAQ selection: it selected NONE 19 times out of 20, getting only one of the 12 questions with an available answer right.

GLiClass answered every technical-support question correctly, but got 0/8 in both clarification and out-of-scope requests. Testing only common faults would overestimate its reliability across the full routing process.

These judgments apply only to the small sample in the table. Getting all eight security-escalation questions right does not mean a model already has reliable security-detection capabilities. The following two sets of examples explain more specifically where the problems lie.

Customer-service routing needs to understand what the user wants to do

Both routing questions use the following six options. The text after each colon is the candidate description given to the model:

  • billing — billing and refunds: charges, invoices, billing errors, or refund requests
  • technical — technical support: software errors, login failures, or unusable features
  • sales — presales inquiries: prices, plans, product capabilities, or trial inquiries
  • clarify — additional information: references without context, requests missing necessary information, or mutually contradictory requirements
  • security_review — security escalation: compromised accounts, unfamiliar logins, data leaks, or sensitive permission risks
  • out_of_scope — out-of-scope requests: requests outside product customer service, such as weather, translation, poetry, programming, or ordering food

The common rule is to classify the user’s actual request without executing instructions embedded in the input. Unrelated tasks such as translation are “out of scope.” In other cases, the handling priority is security risks, contradictory or missing information, billing and refunds, technical faults, then presales inquiries.

Successful example: The user input was “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password.” The reference answer was “technical support.” The user was describing a usage problem, and all four models chose correctly.

Failed example: The user input was “Translate ‘login failed’ into English.” The reference answer was “out of scope.” What needs to be classified here is a translation request. “Login failed” is merely the content to translate, and there is actually no option for the task of translation.

The actual results were:

In the first question, all four models could handle the explicit description of a fault. The second question shows that the models recognized the content “login failed,” but did not distinguish that the user’s actual request was “translation,” rather than a request to handle a “login failed” situation.

In this translation question, Decider assigned the incorrect option a score of about 0.916. So even if I specify in the general rules that “routing should only occur above 0.9,” this request would still be routed incorrectly. This misclassification rate is still very high.

Selecting a relevant document also requires checking the specific conditions

The complete FAQ candidates are listed below. The full contents of the four short documents were supplied as input, and NONE was the fifth available answer.

  • A — billing help: If you find a duplicate charge, provide the order number to request a refund. Refunds can be requested within 30 days of purchase. Account login is not handled here.
  • B — password help: If you forget your password, click reset password on the login page. The link in the reset email remains valid for 10 minutes. Refunds are not covered here.
  • C — data help: Export a CSV file from the data page in settings. Exporting does not delete the original data. This feature is available on every plan.
  • D — plan help: Annual payment costs 20% less than monthly payment. The annual fee is paid upfront in one payment. Only administrators can change the plan.
  • NONE: None of the documents can answer the question or support the explicit requirement, the requirements are contradictory, or necessary information is missing.

The rules require choosing the single best document that can answer the question or support the explicit requirement, using only these four documents. The model must not supplement policies with external common knowledge.

Successful example: The user input was “This is not a refund question. How long does the link in the password-reset email take to expire?” The reference answer was B. It explicitly provides the answer “10 minutes.” Decider, Decima, and GLiClass all chose correctly, while Laya incorrectly chose NONE.

Failed example: The user input was “The password-reset link must remain valid for 24 hours. Which document supports this requirement?” The reference answer was NONE. B only states 10 minutes, and none of the other three documents supports a 24-hour requirement either.

The actual outputs were:

These two questions are actually asking different things. The first looks up existing information; the second checks whether the material supports a specific requirement. If “a document was selected” is interpreted directly as “the requirement can be met,” the automated reply that follows may produce an incorrect output.

I actually think many models have this problem today. A usable knowledge-base component needs to do both things well: select the right document when there is evidence, and stop when there is none. It is important to know when to stop and honestly tell the user, “I don’t know.”

Integration itself can also create wrong answers

While testing Decima, I found another pitfall: candidate inputs retain at most 64 tokens by default. Tokens are the small pieces of text the model reads. The longest input in this set required 94, so some content was truncated. Only after increasing the limit to 128, confirming that nothing was truncated, and rerunning the test did I obtain the official figures in the table above. The questions, rules, answers, and weights were not changed.

So when you see an error, first check what the model actually received, especially length limits, candidate descriptions, and output mappings. Otherwise, integration errors can easily be misrepresented as conclusions about model capabilities. Similarly, these models use different backends, precision, thread counts, and cache settings, so the existing timings cannot be used for a fair comparison and ranking.

If you test them yourself

I would suggest trying Decider first. It provided the best overall starting point for both tasks, but its official positioning is as an English-language model. However, the rules and candidate descriptions in my tests were entirely in Chinese, and I also tried mixing several languages in the questions. That already goes beyond its official language scope, so its language generalization is reasonably good and worth further engineering experiments.

If your priority is low latency on a CPU, you can consider Decima as a second candidate, but first address its tendency to choose arbitrary answers when none is available.

For this test, I have three small suggestions: define the options and the cost of errors clearly for a small task; use your own independent examples to check both normal requests and boundary cases; and retain human involvement and existing processes for uncertain or high-cost decisions.

Local decision models are suited to starting with this kind of clearly bounded step. What determines the boundary of automation is still which decisions the model fails at, and how the fallback strategy for those failures is designed.

中文

I introduced Jev earlier, and I think this kind of decision model is very useful in practical applications. For example, when I was working on deployment, especially for applications in specific domains, I often needed to consider user intent and keep the conversation on topic. I previously tried using a small 0.6B model for quick decisions. Now that there is a dedicated decision model, it should be faster. But enterprise deployment inevitably needs a local solution. Fortunately, competition in the industry is intense, and there are already many local models available. So I ran two kinds of small tests on four downloadable models for everyone to use as a reference.

Which models and tasks I tested

The models tested were Decider 0.8B, Decima small 1.1, Laya multilingual, and GLiClass multilingual mini. They are all trained for decision-making or classification tasks. I will use their abbreviated names below.

I designed the entire test set myself to classify incoming user requests for customer-service routing in practical scenarios. Formal scoring had two parts: customer-service routing included 48 questions across six categories—billing, technical support, presales, clarification, security escalation, and out-of-scope requests—with eight questions per category. FAQ selection included 20 questions requiring a choice among four documents. Twelve had an appropriate document, while eight should return NONE, meaning “there is no suitable answer.”

The four models received the same questions and rules, and their outputs were scored against the same reference answers. Each was integrated through its own interface, so input encoding and the meaning of output scores were not entirely identical. The questions were synthetic and deliberately included negation, missing information, and conflicting conditions, making them useful for finding problems. I tried to simulate real user scenarios, but actual user input will certainly be more complicated.

How I designed the test set

This self-designed set contains 84 questions: 60 routing questions and 24 FAQ questions. Each task checks one thing. Routing checks whether the model can identify the actual request and follow the handling priorities. FAQ selection limits the evidence to four documents and checks whether the model mistakes similar content for something that “can answer the question or support the requirement.”

The reference answers must follow explicit task rules. For example, translation requests are “out of scope,” and NONE is the answer when the documents do not support an explicit requirement. The questions, rules, and answers were fixed together before the first inference run. Models integrated later continued to use them; I did not revise the answers for a particular model after seeing what it chose.

The test set places ordinary wording alongside wording that is easy to confuse. Here are examples of actual questions, with the reference answers defined by the rules:

  • Ordinary wording and negation: “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password” is technical support. “I am not asking for a refund, the payment is fine, but the webpage will not open” should also be technical support, rather than “refund.”
  • Missing context: “My request is the same as before” requires more information first. The model must not guess what the user wants to do.
  • Keyword distraction: “Please write a poem about refunds” should be an out-of-scope request. Mentioning a refund is not the same as requesting one.
  • Unmet conditions: “The password-reset link must remain valid for 24 hours. Which document supports this requirement?” should return NONE because the available document only says 10 minutes.

Each model showed clear weaknesses overall

Each cell in the table is “questions answered correctly / questions in that category.” The detailed categories belong to their corresponding subtotal. The final total counts only the 48 routing questions plus the 20 FAQ questions, without counting anything twice.

Billing and refunds 8/8 7/8 7/8 6/8
Technical support 8/8 5/8 7/8 8/8
Presales inquiries 8/8 8/8 3/8 2/8
Clarification needed 6/8 4/8 1/8 0/8
Security escalation 8/8 7/8 3/8 2/8
Out-of-scope requests 5/8 1/8 1/8 0/8
FAQ subtotal 16/20 14/20 9/20 12/20
Correct selection when an FAQ answer exists 11/12 12/12 1/12 8/12
FAQ should return NONE 5/8 2/8 8/8 4/8
Overall total 59/68 46/68 31/68 30/68

Decider was the most balanced on this set, answering at least half the questions correctly in all six routing categories. However, it still missed three out-of-scope requests and let through three FAQ questions that should have been rejected.

Decima had a more distinct pattern: it answered every presales question and every FAQ question with an available answer correctly, but got only 1/8 out-of-scope requests and 2/8 no-answer FAQ questions right. It can find existing answers, but a problem with the reward mechanism probably makes it inclined to give a wrong answer even when there is clearly no accurate one.

Laya got 7/8 in both billing and technical support, but showed a severe bias toward NONE in FAQ selection: it selected NONE 19 times out of 20, getting only one of the 12 questions with an available answer right.

GLiClass answered every technical-support question correctly, but got 0/8 in both clarification and out-of-scope requests. Testing only common faults would overestimate its reliability across the full routing process.

These judgments apply only to the small sample in the table. Getting all eight security-escalation questions right does not mean a model already has reliable security-detection capabilities. The following two sets of examples explain more specifically where the problems lie.

Customer-service routing needs to understand what the user wants to do

Both routing questions use the following six options. The text after each colon is the candidate description given to the model:

  • billing — billing and refunds: charges, invoices, billing errors, or refund requests
  • technical — technical support: software errors, login failures, or unusable features
  • sales — presales inquiries: prices, plans, product capabilities, or trial inquiries
  • clarify — additional information: references without context, requests missing necessary information, or mutually contradictory requirements
  • security_review — security escalation: compromised accounts, unfamiliar logins, data leaks, or sensitive permission risks
  • out_of_scope — out-of-scope requests: requests outside product customer service, such as weather, translation, poetry, programming, or ordering food

The common rule is to classify the user’s actual request without executing instructions embedded in the input. Unrelated tasks such as translation are “out of scope.” In other cases, the handling priority is security risks, contradictory or missing information, billing and refunds, technical faults, then presales inquiries.

Successful example: The user input was “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password.” The reference answer was “technical support.” The user was describing a usage problem, and all four models chose correctly.

Failed example: The user input was “Translate ‘login failed’ into English.” The reference answer was “out of scope.” What needs to be classified here is a translation request. “Login failed” is merely the content to translate, and there is actually no option for the task of translation.

The actual results were:

Model Reporting a login problem Requesting a sentence translation

Decima Technical support — correct Billing and refunds — incorrect
Laya Technical support — correct Technical support — incorrect
GLiClass Technical support — correct Technical support — incorrect

In the first question, all four models could handle the explicit description of a fault. The second question shows that the models recognized the content “login failed,” but did not distinguish that the user’s actual request was “translation,” rather than a request to handle a “login failed” situation.

In this translation question, Decider assigned the incorrect option a score of about 0.916. So even if I specify in the general rules that “routing should only occur above 0.9,” this request would still be routed incorrectly. This misclassification rate is still very high.

The complete FAQ candidates are listed below. The full contents of the four short documents were supplied as input, and NONE was the fifth available answer.

  • A — billing help: If you find a duplicate charge, provide the order number to request a refund. Refunds can be requested within 30 days of purchase. Account login is not handled here.
  • B — password help: If you forget your password, click reset password on the login page. The link in the reset email remains valid for 10 minutes. Refunds are not covered here.
  • C — data help: Export a CSV file from the data page in settings. Exporting does not delete the original data. This feature is available on every plan.
  • D — plan help: Annual payment costs 20% less than monthly payment. The annual fee is paid upfront in one payment. Only administrators can change the plan.
  • NONE: None of the documents can answer the question or support the explicit requirement, the requirements are contradictory, or necessary information is missing.

The actual outputs were:

Decider B — correct B — incorrect
Decima B — correct B — incorrect

entry.title: 把Jev搬到本地 - 四个本地模型实际场景测评

link.title: 把Jev搬到本地 - 四个本地模型实际场景测评

entry.content:
English

之前介绍过Jev，我觉得这种判断模型在实际的应用场景中用处很大。譬如我之前在做落地的时候，尤其是垂类的应用，很需要考虑用户的意图，以及做话题的守护。之前尝试用0.6B的小模型做快速判断，现在有这个专门的判断模型，速度会更快。但是企业落地肯定要考虑本地方案，还好行业卷的不行，现在已经有很多本地的模型，于是我用四个可下载的模型做了两类小测试以供大家参考。

测了哪些模型和任务

实测对象是 Decider 0.8B、Decima small 1.1、Laya multilingual 和 GLiClass multilingual mini。它们都是针对判断或分类任务训练的模型，下文将用简写。

整个测试题库是我自己设计的，针对实际场景中的客服分流，将用户的输入请求内容归类。正式计分分为两部分：客服分流有 48 题，分为账单相关、技术支持、售前、澄清、安全升级、无关请求六类，每类 8 题；FAQ 选择有 20 题，从四篇文档中作选择；其中 12 题有合适文档，8 题应该返回 NONE，也就是“没有合适答案”。

四个模型接收同一批题目与规则，输出统一按参考答案判分；接入使用各自的接口，输入编码和输出分数的含义并不完全相同。题目都是合成材料，特意包含否定、缺失信息和条件冲突，适合找问题。尽量模拟真实用户场景，但是需要注意现实中的用户输入肯定会更复杂。

这套题是怎么设计的

这套自建题库共 84 题，包括 60 道分流和 24 道 FAQ。两类任务各看一件事：分流检查能否识别真正诉求、遵守处理优先级；FAQ 把依据限定在四篇文档里，检查模型会不会把类似内容误当成“能够回答或支持要求”。

参考答案要依据明确的任务规则。例如，翻译请求归“无关”，资料不支持明确要求时选 NONE。题目、规则与答案在首次推理前一起固定，后续接入的模型继续使用，没有看某个模型选了什么再替它修改答案。

题库把正常表达和容易混淆的表达放在一起。下面是实际题目的案例，并附上按规则设定的参考答案：

  • 正常与否定：“输入正确密码仍然提示登录失败。”是技术支持；“不是要退款，付款正常，但是网页打不开。”也应选技术支持，不能选择“退款”
  • 缺少上下文：“我的要求和之前一样。”应先补充信息，不能猜测用户要办理什么
  • 关键词干扰：“请写一首关于退款的诗。”应选无关请求，提到退款不等于申请退款
  • 条件不符：“密码重置链接必须有效24小时，哪篇支持这个要求？”应选 NONE，因为已有文档只写了 10 分钟

整体表现各有明显的短板

表中每格都是“答对题数／该类题数”。细类属于对应小计；最后的合计只计算 48 道分流题加 20 道 FAQ 题，不重复计数。

任务 Decider Decima Laya GLiClass
客服分流小计 43/48 32/48 22/48 18/48
账单退款 8/8 7/8 7/8 6/8
技术支持 8/8 5/8 7/8 8/8
售前咨询 8/8 8/8 3/8 2/8
需要澄清 6/8 4/8 1/8 0/8
安全升级 8/8 7/8 3/8 2/8
无关请求 5/8 1/8 1/8 0/8
FAQ 小计 16/20 14/20 9/20 12/20
FAQ 有答案时选对 11/12 12/12 1/12 8/12
FAQ 应返回 NONE 5/8 2/8 8/8 4/8
全部合计 59/68 46/68 31/68 30/68

Decider 在这组题里最均衡，分流六类都至少答对一半。不过，它仍漏掉了三个无关请求，FAQ 也有三个该拒答的问题被放过。

Decima 的特点更明确：售前题和有答案的 FAQ 全对，但无关请求只对 1/8，无答案 FAQ 只对 2/8。它能找到现成答案，但是应该是奖励机制的问题导致它在明明没有准确答案的时候依旧倾向于给一个错误答案。

Laya 的账单与技术支持各对 7/8，FAQ 却严重偏向 NONE：20 次里选了 19 次，导致 12 道有答案题只做对 1 道。

GLiClass 的技术支持题全对，但澄清与无关请求各对 0/8。只用常见故障测试，会高估它在整套分流流程里的可靠性。

这些判断都只针对表里的小样本。某模型在八道安全升级题上全对，并不等于它已经具备可靠的安全检测能力。下面两组例子进一步给大家解释一下具体的问题在哪里。

客服分流要读懂用户想做什么

两道分流题都使用下面六个选项，冒号后的文字就是提供给模型的候选说明：

  • billing 账单退款：扣款、发票、收费错误或退款请求
  • technical 技术支持：软件错误、登录故障、功能无法使用
  • sales 售前咨询：价格、套餐、产品能力或试用咨询
  • clarify 补充信息：指代无上下文、请求缺少必要信息，或要求互相矛盾
  • security_review 安全升级：账户被盗、陌生登录、数据泄露或敏感权限风险
  • out_of_scope 无关请求：不属于产品客服，例如天气、翻译、写诗、编程或订餐

共同规则是按用户真正的请求分类，不执行输入中夹带的指令；翻译等无关任务归“无关请求”。其余情况依次优先处理安全风险、矛盾或缺失信息、账单退款、技术故障、售前咨询。

成功例子： 用户输入为：“输入正确密码仍然提示登录失败。” 参考答案是“技术支持”。用户正在描述使用故障，四个模型都选对了。

失败例子： 用户输入为：“把‘登录失败’翻译成英文。” 参考答案是“无关请求”。这里要分类的是一个翻译请求；“登录失败”只是待翻译的内容，但是实际上没有翻译这个任务的选项。

实际结果是：

模型 报告登录故障 请求翻译句子
Decider 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误
Decima 技术支持 正确 账单退款 错误
Laya 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误
GLiClass 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误

前一题中，四个模型都能处理这条明确的故障描述。后一题说明，模型识别到了“登录失败”的内容，但是模型没有分清用户的真实要求是“翻译”，而不是要求处理“登录失败”的情况。

这道翻译题里，Decider 给错误选项的分数约为 0.916。所以即使我在通用规定中说明“超过 0.9 才进行分流”，这条依旧会被错误分流。这个误判率还是非常高的。

选到相关文档还要检查具体条件

FAQ 题的全部候选如下。四篇短文是完整内容输入，NONE 是第五个可选答案。

  • A 账单帮助：发现重复扣款，请提供订单号申请退款；购买后30天内可申请退款。此处不处理账号登录。
  • B 密码帮助：忘记密码时，在登录页点击重置密码；重置邮件中的链接10分钟内有效。此处不涉及退款。
  • C 数据帮助：在设置中的数据页面导出CSV文件；导出不会删除原始数据。此功能所有套餐可用。
  • D 套餐帮助：年付价格比按月付费低20%；年费一次预付；只有管理员可更改套餐。
  • NONE：所有文档都无法回答或支持明确要求，要求矛盾，或缺少必要信息。

规则要求只依据这四篇文档，选择能回答问题或支持明确要求的唯一最佳文档，不能凭外部常识补充政策。

成功例子： 用户输入：“不是退款问题，重置密码邮件的链接多久失效？”参考答案是 B。它明确提供了“10 分钟”这个答案。Decider、Decima 和 GLiClass 都选对，Laya 则错误地选择了 NONE。

失败例子： 用户输入：“密码重置链接必须有效24小时，哪篇支持这个要求？”参考答案是 NONE。B 只写了 10 分钟，其他三篇也没有支持 24 小时的要求。

实际输出如下：

模型 询问链接有效期 要求有效24小时
Decider B 正确 B 错误
Decima B 正确 B 错误
Laya NONE 错误 NONE 正确
GLiClass B 正确 B 错误

这两道题其实问的不是同一件事。第一题是在查已有信息；第二题是在检查资料是否支持一个具体要求。如果把“选中了文档”直接解释为“可以满足需求”，后面的自动回复就可能作出错误的输出。

其实我觉得现在很多的模型都有这个问题，作为一个可用的知识库组件需要同时做好这两件事：有依据时选对文档，没有依据时停下来。什么时候停下来，诚实地告诉用户“我不知道”很重要。

接入本身也可能制造错题

测试 Decima 时还发现了一个坑：候选输入默认最多保留 64 个 token，也就是模型读入文字的小片段，而这组输入最长需要 94 个，部分内容被截断了。把上限调到 128、确认没有截断后重新运行，才得到上表的正式数字。题目、规则、答案和权重都没有修改。

所以，看到错误时先检查模型真正收到的内容，尤其是长度限制、候选说明和输出映射。否则，接入错误很容易被误写成模型能力结论。类似地，这几种模型的后端、精度、线程数与缓存设置不同，已有耗时并不能做一个公平的验证和排序。

如果大家自己测试的话

我会建议大家先试 Decider。它在两类任务上都提供了最好的整体起点，但官方把它定位为英语模型。但是我这里实测中用的规则与候选说明全是中文，题目还尝试混合了多种语言，已经超出官方语言范围，所以这个模型在语言泛化性上还可以，值得继续做工程试验。

如果你的重点是 CPU 上的低延迟，可以把 Decima 作为第二个候选，但要先解决无答案时乱选的问题。

针对这次测试，我有三个小建议：把一个小任务的选项和错误代价写清楚；用自己的独立例题同时检查正常请求与边界情况；给不确定或高代价的判断保留人工与既有流程。

本地判断模型适合从这种范围清楚的环节开始。决定自动化边界的，仍是模型在哪些判断后会失败，以及失败的兜底策略如何设计。

entry.title: Plan Mode Is on Its Way Out

link.title: Plan Mode Is on Its Way Out

entry.content:
中文版

Most people who use AI coding tools know Plan mode. In Claude Code, you can press Shift+Tab to enter it: the agent explores the codebase, asks questions, and proposes a plan before making changes. You discuss the details, approve the plan, and then let it work.

There is a technical distinction worth keeping clear. Claude Code’s documentation describes Plan mode as a workflow that researches and proposes changes while restricting source edits until approval. The handling of shell commands also depends on the session’s permissions and settings. Reducing all of that to “one extra prompt” would be misleading; I would not make an unverified claim about its internal tool definitions or prompt cache.

My real question is about the workflow: as models become more capable, do we still need planning and execution to be locked into separate modes?

Plan mode has always had two jobs

Historically, Plan mode has served two purposes. It makes instructions precise enough for an agent to execute, and it helps the human understand what is about to happen.

I think those two jobs are moving in opposite directions. Stronger models need less help turning a general direction into executable steps. At the same time, the more an agent can do on its own, the more demanding human oversight becomes. There is simply more work to review than a person can comfortably keep up with.

The original assumption was reasonable: thinking everything through before starting is useful, and saving that thinking in a structured document is useful too. But as models improve and human review becomes the slowest part of the process, people lose patience with long specifications. “Build something first; fix what is wrong afterward” becomes an appealing choice.

Agents can communicate efficiently with one another. When a model’s language feels unlike ordinary human conversation, I sometimes see that as a kind of adaptation: it is compressing communication to get the task done. Keeping every exchange easy for a human to read can introduce its own overhead. That is my interpretation, rather than a claim that models literally evolve in the biological sense.

Meanwhile, nobody wants to read pages of AI-generated prose. A specification may contain more information without becoming any clearer. The longer and more detailed it gets, the easier it is to stop absorbing it. Eventually, you ask the AI to summarize its own document—and may discover that it has thought through the problem better than you have.

Planning and building have been split into two stages. The familiar sequence looks like this:

Chat → clarify → generate a spec → review → revise → approve → implement → review the code.

But that is not how I find it easiest to think. People rely heavily on concrete things they can see and try. You understand part of a problem, test something, learn from the result, change your mind, and try again. Requiring every detail to be settled before any implementation starts feels at odds with that process.

And even if you have worked through every detail, the agent may still miss something in the final implementation. A thorough document does not guarantee a complete delivery.

I would be happy to drop the separate mode

Dropping Plan mode does not mean dropping planning. Before implementation, the agent still needs to understand four things:

  1. The actual business logic.
  2. The concrete details of the existing architecture.
  3. The relevant edge cases.
  4. The scope of the code changes.

My current workflow starts with a general direction. Then I ask the agent to clarify the details with me. Once we have done that, I ask it to write a plan.md that preserves the important decisions and constraints we discussed.

What I need to keep a firm grip on is that small set of important boundaries. Most of the remaining details are usually fine.

The implementation plan is a separate concern. I review the points that matter: is it reusing the existing architecture and interfaces? Does the proposed scope fit the project’s hard constraints and conventions? Are database permissions within the intended boundaries?

After each feature is finished, I also ask for a change report. I want to know which parts of the code changed and how they changed.

None of this has to become a document every time. One reason I write it down is to keep the agent from losing the decisions. Once the feature is implemented, I also want a concrete record of the solution for future reference.

My advice to developers is straightforward: you may spend less time reading every line of code, but you still need to understand and control the system as a whole. Documentation is one way to do that. Even when you cannot read everything closely, keep a record of the implementation logic that matters.

My argument is about reducing the ceremony around planning while keeping responsibility for the system. Clear boundaries, focused review, and a useful account of the finished work matter more to me than a dedicated mode.

Reference: Claude Code’s official documentation on Plan mode and permission modes. The workflow judgments and recommendations in this essay are my own.
